content:
The image shows a corn ear with the husk partially pulled back, revealing:

- Yellow kernels with extensive **green/teal-colored mold** growing over the surface of the ear
- The mold appears powdery/fuzzy in texture, covering patches across the kernels
- The husks are dry and brown (mature/late-season corn)
- White mycelium is also visible at the base/tip of the ear

Key evidence: The **green/teal powdery mold** on corn kernels is the hallmark of **Trichoderma ear rot**, caused by *Trichoderma* spp., which produces distinctive blue-green to dark green mycelium on infected ears. This is distinct from Diplodia (white mold), Gibberella (pink/red mold), or Aspergillus (olive-green powdery mold that tends to be more localized at the tip).

The color here — teal-green, relatively uniform across the ear surface — strongly points to Trichoderma rather than Aspergillus (which would be more olive/yellowish-green and tip-focused) or Fusarium (pinkish).
